blocks.md:
This lesson follows **Where the Hours Go: Quantifying the ML Lifecycle** in *ML Lifecycle* (Vol I). By the end you should be able to:

- Analyze the primary empirical time sinks reported by ML practitioners in the chapter's survey analysis
- Trace late-discovery rework through dependent data, model, validation, and deployment artifacts

blocks.source: Vol I, ML Lifecycle, § Where the Hours Go: Quantifying the ML Lifecycle
blocks.md: The DR team lost five months to one late constraint. Conceptual models of the ML lifecycle describe which stages exist, but planning a workflow requires knowing where its hours go, and that time rarely concentrates where research literature spends its pages.

blocks.title: Map of the section
blocks.md: Pay attention to: Practitioner time allocation across data and modeling work.

blocks.prompt: Think first: A DR team's validation pipeline takes a full week per candidate model. Using the chapter's iteration tax, explain what this slow loop costs the team beyond calendar time, and name the workflow mechanism the chapter proposes to keep late discoveries from multiplying that cost.
blocks.md: A week-long loop limits how many candidate models the team can test in a fixed period, so the team explores a much narrower part of the design space and learns less about which data, preprocessing, and architecture choices matter. That lost search breadth is the iteration tax. Late discoveries amplify it, because a violation caught after deployment invalidates artifacts produced by earlier stages and forces retraining and renewed validation. The chapter's remedy is explicit stage interface contracts that validate each stage's outputs at its boundary, so violations surface where they are cheapest to fix.

questions.q: In the 2016 CrowdFlower data scientist survey cited in the text, respondents indicated that data-related tasks dominated their time, with 60 percent selecting ____ and organizing data as their largest time sink, compared to only 4 percent for refining algorithms.
questions.explanation: cleaning. Cleaning and organizing data accounted for 60 percent of most-time responses, and collecting datasets accounted for 19 percent. Most respondents therefore named one of these data activities as their largest time sink. These response shares do not measure the fraction of total engineering hours spent on each activity.
